description:
We are a team of young Romanian high school students united by our curiosity for technology and science. Bringing together experience in software engineering, product development, design, and astrophysics, we enjoy turning complex ideas into accessible, functional tools. 

Through Flickering Pixels, we aim to combine our technical skills and curiosity to make the changing universe easier to explore, bringing astronomical observations closer to researchers, students, and space enthusiasts alike.
summary:
Flickering Pixels is an immersive web experience powered by NASA’s SPHEREx space telescope, offering innovative features for both amateur astronomers and experts in the field. We directly addressed the lack of an interactive, user-friendly tool by combining three separate capabilities into a single platform, composed by 3 main functionalities: Sky-Map, Data-Analysis and Spatial Art Gallery.

First, our project includes a Google Maps-like view of the all-sky SPHEREx surveys, allowing users to explore the sky freely and watch the sky flicker over time. Users can inspect detailed object data, flag suspicious moving objects, or share specific coordinates with other passionate astronomers. 

Second, we provide a data analysis tool featuring an adjustable FoV, custom frame counts, and a spectrum viewer. Users can also download any desired GIFs, FITS, or PNGs.

Third, our Spatial Art Gallery showcases daily featured astronomical observations alongside 3D sculptures generated from pixel light intensity. This feature offers an intuitive, visual entry point for anyone interested in the artistic side of astronomy.
details:
Flickering Pixels is designed around three main concepts that work together to transform the way people explore, understand and interact with real NASA data. Rather than being just an ordinary viewing tool, our platform combines the functionality of a navigation system, a scientific data-analysis tool and an interactive digital art gallery. Each concept has a different purpose, but together they create a complete experience that makes exploring the universe more intuitive, educational and visually engaging. 

1. Sky-Map

The first concept behind Flickering Pixels is to create something similar to Google Maps or Google Earth, but instead of exploring cities, countries and geographical locations, users can explore the universe. Just as Google Maps allows people to search for a specific address and navigate to a location on Earth, our platform allows users to select specific regions of the sky using astronomical coordinates, specifically Right Ascension and Declination. The goal is to make astronomical exploration feel familiar, even for people who have never worked with scientific data before. Users should not need to understand complicated astronomical software or manually search through enormous databases to find a particular region of space. Instead, they can simply enter a famous star’s name or choose a known location and let the platform retrieve the available observations for that area. 

By connecting the platform to NASA's SPHEREx observations through the Infrared Science Archive (IRSA), Flickering Pixels provides access to real astronomical data associated with the selected coordinates. Users can explore different regions of the sky, discover what has been observed and investigate the same location across different observation periods. 

Users can view any patch of the sky at either the first or last visit, or blink between frames to see how objects move over time. By right-clicking anywhere on the sky, users can select “What’s here?” and get detailed information about the selected object, along with catalog data from Gaia and ALLWISE. Moreover, users can either open their Field of View in Target LAB, flag the object as a possible mover if it isn’t already cataloged as a high-proper-motion star or a known asteroid/comet, or even click “Share this spot” and get a shareable link that opens the Sky-Map at those exact coordinates.

2. Data-Analysis Tool

Another function of our website is the Target LAB, which is useful for users who want to access the data behind SPHEREx images. The interface features a quick target search and precise controls for Right Ascension, Declination, Field of View, and frame sequences, making complex sky data accessible to users at any experience level. The images are shown in a preview in the center of the screen, allowing users to inspect any object clearly.

Users can search for their preferred object not only by name, but also by Declination and Right Ascension, and switch between seven spectral filters (D1-D6 and RGB) while viewing key metadata (name, type) and predicting the motion of moving objects.

Users can also add a bookmark to a certain object in order to save it and access it more easily and quickly. A new tool aimed at professionals is the option to download data directly from the telescope's output, either by getting the PNG image shown in the preview, extracting the folder with all the FITS stacked in the image, downloading the GIFs that shows movement over time, or by analyzing the spectrum of the object shown.

3. Spatial Art Gallery

The Spatial Art Gallery concept focuses on turning scientific observations into an immersive visual experience. The blinking functionality also introduces a dynamic element, making the universe appear alive as astronomical objects shift or change between observations. This approach can make astronomy more attractive to people who might not initially be interested in scientific analysis, including students, artists and general audiences. Our idea is that users should be able to open Flickering Pixels simply out of curiosity, explore beautiful astronomical images, discover interesting structures and gradually develop an interest in the science behind them.

We want to take advantage of this visual potential and make astronomical data something that people can explore not only scientifically, but also aesthetically. Rather than limiting users strictly to raw datasets and technical interfaces, the gallery gives them an opportunity to interact with astronomical imagery and appreciate the visual complexity of the universe.

The sculptures (the two 3D elevation models displayed in the gallery) each represent a patch of the sky viewed through one of the detector bands (D1-D6) and the height is determined by pixel luminance. Peaks are adjusted to be smoother and the color gradient goes from light blue (low elevation) to white (highest elevation).
